pages.text: Soil is a mix of $(thing)sand$() (gritty, drains fast, holds little), $(thing)silt$() (smooth, holds water well) and $(thing)clay$() (sticky, holds water and nutrients but drains slowly). The mix decides the texture class, one of the twelve USDA classes, plus $(thing)peat$().
$(thing)Sand and loamy sand$() warm up early and are easy to work, but dry out fast, lose nitrogen to leaching and need frequent manure.
$(thing)Loams$() (loam, silt loam, sandy loam) are the best all-round farm soils: good water, good drainage and good fertility.
$(thing)Clays$() hold the most water and nutrients but stay wet and cold in spring, compact easily and smear if worked wet.
$(thing)Peat$() is half organic matter. It forms in cold, wet hollows, holds huge amounts of water and is naturally very acidic.
Texture also sets how far water seeps sideways from a ditch or pond: about two blocks through sand and up to five or six through silts, clays and peat. Fine soils draw water by capillarity.
